# Ridge and lasso

3. (8 pts)
Using the cardiovascular mortality regression data, form lagged features from
the particulate matter and temperature variables, using lags 4, 8, ..., 40 from 
each. Using the `glmnet` package, fit a ridge regression and lasso regression
(two separate models), each over a grid of tuning parameter values $\lambda$ 
chosen by the `glmnet()` function, with cardiovascular mortality as the response
and all the lagged features as predictors (you should have 20 in total: 10 from
particulate matter, and 10 from temperature). However, make sure you do this in
a split-sample setup for validation, as follows, for each of ridge and lasso:

- fit the model on the *first half of the time series*; 
- make predictions on the *second half of the time series*, for each $\lambda$;
- record the MAE of the predictions on the second half, for each $\lambda$;
- choose and report the value of $\lambda$ with the lowest MAE;
- plot the cardiovascular mortality time series, along with the predictions on 
  the second half, and print the MAE and the selected value of $\lambda$ on the 
  plot.

    You can build on the code from the regularization lecture for fitting the ridge 
    and lasso models, and the regression lecture for the split-sample validation. 
    *Note carefully that the lecture code includes lag 0, and here we do not, so 
    that we can make ex-ante 4-week ahead forecasts!*

```{python}
# Create lagged features
lags = list(range(4, 40, 4))
df = pd.DataFrame({"mort": cmort["value"]})
for lag in lags:
    df[f"part_lag{lag}"] = part["value"].shift(lag)
    df[f"temp_lag{lag}"] = tempr["value"].shift(lag)

df = df.dropna().reset_index(drop=True)
n = len(df)
n_half = n // 2

# Train-test split
train_df = df.iloc[:n_half]
test_df = df.iloc[n_half:]

X_train = train_df.drop(columns=["mort"])
y_train = train_df["mort"]
X_test = test_df.drop(columns=["mort"])
y_test = test_df["mort"]

# Standardize predictors using training set scaling
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

# glmnet-style grid anchored at alpha_max (smallest lambda that zeroes all lasso coefs)
alpha_max = np.max(np.abs(X_train_scaled.T @ y_train)) / len(y_train)
lambdas_lasso = np.logspace(np.log10(alpha_max * 1e-4), np.log10(alpha_max), 200)
lambdas_ridge = np.logspace(np.log10(alpha_max * 1e-4), np.log10(alpha_max * 1e4), 200)

# Lasso
lasso_maes = []
for lam in lambdas_lasso:
    model = Lasso(alpha=lam, max_iter=10000)
    model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
    preds = model.predict(X_test_scaled)
    lasso_maes.append(mean_absolute_error(y_test, preds))

best_idx_l = np.argmin(lasso_maes)
best_lambda_l = lambdas_lasso[best_idx_l]
best_mae_l = lasso_maes[best_idx_l]

# Optimal Lasso predictions
best_lasso = Lasso(alpha=best_lambda_l, max_iter=10000)
best_lasso.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
lasso_preds = best_lasso.predict(X_test_scaled)

# Ridge
ridge_maes = []
for lam in lambdas_ridge:
    model = Ridge(alpha=lam)
    model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
    preds = model.predict(X_test_scaled)
    ridge_maes.append(mean_absolute_error(y_test, preds))

best_idx_r = np.argmin(ridge_maes)
best_lambda_r = lambdas_ridge[best_idx_r]
best_mae_r = ridge_maes[best_idx_r]

# Optimal Ridge predictions
best_ridge = Ridge(alpha=best_lambda_r)
best_ridge.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
ridge_preds = best_ridge.predict(X_test_scaled)

# Plot Lasso and Ridge split-sample results
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4))
sns.lineplot(x=df.index, y=df["mort"], color="grey", alpha=0.6, ax=ax, label="Observed")
sns.lineplot(x=test_df.index, y=lasso_preds, color="tomato", ax=ax, label=f"Lasso ($\\lambda$={best_lambda_l:.4f}, MAE={best_mae_l:.3f})")
sns.lineplot(x=test_df.index, y=ridge_preds, linestyle="--", color="steelblue", ax=ax, label=f"Ridge ($\\lambda$={best_lambda_r:.4f}, MAE={best_mae_r:.3f})")
ax.axvline(x=n_half, color="black", linestyle="--")
ax.set_title("Split-Sample: Lasso vs. Ridge Predictions")
ax.set_xlabel("Week Index")
ax.set_ylabel("Cardiovascular Mortality")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

5. (8 pts)
Repeat Q3, except implement time series cross-validation instead of split-sample 
validation. You should begin time series cross-validation on the second half of
the time series, treating the first half as a burn-in set. Also, be sure to fit 
each ridge or lasso model using a trailing window of 200 time points (not all 
past). 

    Note that in Python, we pass explicit `lambda` parameters to scikit-learn models 
    ahead of time, which naturally circumvents the variable tuning grid issues 
    seen in R. We can use the same `lambdas_lasso` and `lambdas_ridge` grids defined in Q3.
    Produce plots of the cardiovascular mortality time series, along with the 
    predictions from time series CV on the second half, and print the MAE and 
    the selected value of $\lambda$ on the plots.

```{python}
tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)

lasso_cv_preds = []
ridge_cv_preds = []
lasso_alphas_selected = []
ridge_alphas_selected = []
lasso_coefs_history = []
y_cv_true = []

# Rolling TS CV loop using LassoCV / RidgeCV for adaptive lambda selection
for t in range(n_half, n):
    window = df.iloc[t-200:t]
    X_tr = window.drop(columns=["mort"])
    y_tr = window["mort"]
    X_te = df.iloc[[t]].drop(columns=["mort"])
    y_cv_true.append(df.loc[t, "mort"])

    scaler_cv = StandardScaler()
    X_tr_scaled = scaler_cv.fit_transform(X_tr)
    X_te_scaled = scaler_cv.transform(X_te)

    lasso_model = LassoCV(alphas=lambdas_lasso, cv=tscv, max_iter=5000)
    lasso_model.fit(X_tr_scaled, y_tr)
    lasso_cv_preds.append(lasso_model.predict(X_te_scaled)[0])
    lasso_alphas_selected.append(lasso_model.alpha_)
    lasso_coefs_history.append(lasso_model.coef_)

    ridge_model = RidgeCV(alphas=lambdas_ridge, cv=tscv)
    ridge_model.fit(X_tr_scaled, y_tr)
    ridge_cv_preds.append(ridge_model.predict(X_te_scaled)[0])
    ridge_alphas_selected.append(ridge_model.alpha_)

best_lasso_cv_preds = lasso_cv_preds
best_ridge_cv_preds = ridge_cv_preds
best_mae_cv_l = mean_absolute_error(y_cv_true, lasso_cv_preds)
best_mae_cv_r = mean_absolute_error(y_cv_true, ridge_cv_preds)
best_lambda_cv_l = np.median(lasso_alphas_selected)
best_lambda_cv_r = np.median(ridge_alphas_selected)

# Plot Lasso and Ridge CV predictions
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4))
sns.lineplot(x=df.index, y=df["mort"], color="grey", alpha=0.6, ax=ax, label="Observed")
sns.lineplot(x=df.index[n_half:], y=best_lasso_cv_preds, color="tomato", ax=ax, label=f"Lasso ($\\lambda$={best_lambda_cv_l:.4f}, MAE={best_mae_cv_l:.3f})")
sns.lineplot(x=df.index[n_half:], y=best_ridge_cv_preds, linestyle="--", color="steelblue", ax=ax, label=f"Ridge ($\\lambda$={best_lambda_cv_r:.4f}, MAE={best_mae_cv_r:.3f})")
ax.axvline(x=n_half, color="black", linestyle="--")
ax.set_title("TS Cross-Validation: Lasso vs. Ridge Predictions")
ax.set_xlabel("Week Index")
ax.set_ylabel("Cardiovascular Mortality")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# HP filter

7. (5 pts)
Recall in lecture we saw the HP filter could be written explicitly as
$$
\hat\theta = \underbrace{(I + \lambda D^T D)^{-1}}_K \, y,
$$
where $D \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-2) \times n}$ is the second difference matrix on $n$
points. In other words, defining $K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ as above,
$$
\hat\theta_i = \sum_{j=1}^n K_{ij} y_j, \quad i = 1,\dots,n.
$$
Compute the matrix $K$ empirically for a problem of size $n=100$, and setting 
the tuning parameter to be $\lambda=100$; inspect three of its rows, at indices
$i = 25, 50, 75$. For each $i$, plot the $i^{\text{th}}$ row as a curve over the 
underlying position $1,\dots,n$; that is, plot the x-y pairs

$$
(x_j, y_j) = (j, K_{ij}), \quad j = 1,\dots,n
$$

as a curve. Overlay the curves for all three rows on the same plot, each in a 
different color. What do these curves look like to you? Use the plot to argue

# Trend filter

9. (Bonus)
Implement 5-fold cross-validation in order to tune $\lambda$ in trend filtering
applied to the Boston marathon men's data set. Recall the description of how to
set folds in a special "structured" way, for tuning smoothers, given near the 
end of the lecture notes (weeks 5-6: "Regularization and smoothing"). The code
below shows how to run trend filtering and derive estimates at the held-out
points for one fold. You can build off this code for your solution. You will 
need to install the `glmgen` package from GitHub, which you can do using the 
code that has been commented out. 

    Important note: just like `glmnet()`, the `trendfilter()`  function (in the
`glmnet` package) computes its own `lambda` sequence. So you will need to define 
an initial `lambda` sequence to pass to each subsequent call to `trendfilter()`,
so that you can have a consistent grid of tuning parameter values over which to
perform cross-validation. We do this below by using the `lambda` sequence that
`trendfilter()` itself derived when the trend filtering model is fit on the full
data set.

    After implementing cross-validation, compute and report the $\lambda$ value
with the smallest cross-validated MAE. Then, lastly, plot the solution at this
value of $\lambda$ when the model is fit to the full data set (this is already
available in the `tf` object below.)

```{python}
# Load and preprocess data
boston = pd.read_csv("boston_marathon.csv")
boston = boston[(boston["Year"] >= 1924) & (boston["Event"] == "Men's open division")].copy()

def time_to_minutes(t_str):
    parts = list(map(float, t_str.split(':')))
    return parts[0] * 60 + parts[1] + parts[2] / 60

boston["Minutes"] = boston["Time"].apply(time_to_minutes)
x_b = boston["Year"].values
y_b = boston["Minutes"].values
n_b = len(x_b)

def make_D2(x_grid):
    ng = len(x_grid)
    D = np.zeros((ng - 2, ng))
    for i in range(ng - 2):
        h0 = x_grid[i+1] - x_grid[i]
        h1 = x_grid[i+2] - x_grid[i+1]
        scale = x_grid[i+2] - x_grid[i]
        D[i, i] = 1.0 / (scale * h0)
        D[i, i+1] = - (1.0 / h0 + 1.0 / h1) / scale
        D[i, i+2] = 1.0 / (scale * h1)
    return D

def fit_tf(x_grid, y_grid, lmbda):
    ng = len(x_grid)
    theta = cp.Variable(ng)
    D = make_D2(x_grid)
    obj = cp.Minimize(0.5 * cp.sum_squares(y_grid - theta) + lmbda * cp.norm1(D @ theta))
    prob = cp.Problem(obj)
    prob.solve(solver=cp.CLARABEL)
    return theta.value

# 5-fold cross-validation
k_folds = 5
inds = np.array([i % k_folds for i in range(n_b)]) # rep_len(1:k, n) equivalent
lambdas_tf = np.logspace(-2, 3, 50)

cv_maes_tf = []
for lmbda in lambdas_tf:
    fold_maes = []
    for j in range(k_folds):
        train_mask = inds != j
        test_mask = inds == j
        
        x_tr, y_tr = x_b[train_mask], y_b[train_mask]
        x_te, y_te = x_b[test_mask], y_b[test_mask]
        
        # Fit trend filter on training slice
        theta_tr = fit_tf(x_tr, y_tr, lmbda)
        # Evaluate predictions at held-out years using linear interpolation
        yhat = np.interp(x_te, x_tr, theta_tr)
        
        fold_maes.append(mean_absolute_error(y_te, yhat))
    cv_maes_tf.append(np.mean(fold_maes))

best_idx_tf = np.argmin(cv_maes_tf)
best_lambda_tf = lambdas_tf[best_idx_tf]
best_mae_tf = cv_maes_tf[best_idx_tf]

# Fit full model
theta_full = fit_tf(x_b, y_b, best_lambda_tf)

print(f"Optimal Lambda: {best_lambda_tf:.4f}")
print(f"Smallest CV MAE: {best_mae_tf:.4f}")

# Plot solution
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.scatterplot(x=x_b, y=y_b, color="grey", alpha=0.6, label="Observed Minutes", ax=ax)
sns.lineplot(x=x_b, y=theta_full, color="tomato", lw=2.5, label=f"Trend Filter ($\\lambda$={best_lambda_tf:.2f})", ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Boston Marathon Men's Open Division Trend Filtering")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Time (Minutes)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

12. (3 pts)
Recall the code from lecture that performs time series cross-validation to 
evaluate the mean absolute error (MAE) of predictions from the linear regression
of cardiovascular mortality on 4-week lagged particulate levels. Adapt this to 
evaluate the MAE of predictions from the regression of cardiovascular mortality 
on 4-week lagged particulate levels and 4-week lagged temperature (2 features).
Fit each regression model using a trailing window of 200 time points (not all 
past). Plot the predictions, and print the MAE on the plot, following the code
from lecture.

    Additionally (all drawn on the same figure), plot the fitted values on the
    training set (burn-in set, times 1 through $t_0$). The fitted values should 
    come from the initial regression model fit to the burn-in set, plotted in a 
    different color. Print the training MAE on the plot.

```{python}
# Prepare data
df12 = pd.DataFrame({
    "mort": cmort["value"],
    "part4": part["value"].shift(4),
    "temp4": tempr["value"].shift(4)
}).dropna().reset_index(drop=True)

n12 = len(df12)
t0 = 200

# Burn-in fit
fit0_12 = LinearRegression()
fit0_12.fit(df12.iloc[:t0][["part4", "temp4"]], df12.iloc[:t0]["mort"])
train_fitted12 = fit0_12.predict(df12.iloc[:t0][["part4", "temp4"]])
train_mae12 = mean_absolute_error(df12.iloc[:t0]["mort"], train_fitted12)

# TS CV rolling window
preds12 = np.zeros(n12)
preds12[:t0] = np.nan
for t in range(t0, n12):
    window = df12.iloc[t-200:t]
    X_tr = window[["part4", "temp4"]]
    y_tr = window["mort"]
    X_te = df12.iloc[[t]][["part4", "temp4"]]
    
    model = LinearRegression()
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    preds12[t] = model.predict(X_te)[0]

cv_mae12 = mean_absolute_error(df12.iloc[t0:]["mort"], preds12[t0:])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
sns.lineplot(x=df12.index, y=df12["mort"], color="grey", alpha=0.6, label="Observed", ax=ax)
sns.lineplot(x=df12.index[:t0], y=train_fitted12, color="steelblue", lw=2, label="Training Fit (Burn-in)", ax=ax)
sns.lineplot(x=df12.index[t0:], y=preds12[t0:], color="tomato", lw=2, label="CV Predictions", ax=ax)
ax.set_title(f"Q12 (2 features) | CV MAE = {cv_mae12:.2f} | Training MAE = {train_mae12:.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Index")
ax.set_ylabel("Cardiovascular Mortality")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
df14 = pd.DataFrame(df_dict).dropna().reset_index(drop=True)

features14 = [f"part{k}" for k in lag_seq] + [f"temp{k}" for k in lag_seq]

# Burn-in fit
fit0_14 = LinearRegression()
fit0_14.fit(df14.iloc[:t0][features14], df14.iloc[:t0]["mort"])
train_fitted14 = fit0_14.predict(df14.iloc[:t0][features14])
train_mae14 = mean_absolute_error(df14.iloc[:t0]["mort"], train_fitted14)

# TS CV rolling window
preds14 = np.zeros(n14)
preds14[:t0] = np.nan
for t in range(t0, n14):
    window = df14.iloc[t-200:t]
    X_tr = window[features14]
    y_tr = window["mort"]
    X_te = df14.iloc[[t]][features14]
    
    model = LinearRegression()
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    preds14[t] = model.predict(X_te)[0]

cv_mae14 = mean_absolute_error(df14.iloc[t0:]["mort"], preds14[t0:])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
sns.lineplot(x=df14.index, y=df14["mort"], color="grey", alpha=0.6, label="Observed", ax=ax)
sns.lineplot(x=df14.index[:t0], y=train_fitted14, color="steelblue", lw=2, label="Training Fit (Burn-in)", ax=ax)
sns.lineplot(x=df14.index[t0:], y=preds14[t0:], color="tomato", lw=2, label="CV Predictions", ax=ax)
ax.set_title(f"Q14 (94 features) | CV MAE = {cv_mae14:.2f} | Training MAE = {train_mae14:.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Index")
ax.set_ylabel("Cardiovascular Mortality")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

15. (2 pts)

feature vector, for $i = 1,\dots,n$. Let

$$
\tilde{x}_i = (x_{i1}, \dots, x_{ip}, \tilde{x}_{i,p+1}),\quad i = 1,\dots,n
$$

be the result of appending one more feature. Let $\hat{y}_i$ denote the fitted
